 T-Mobile Again Rejects A Network Deal With SpaceX, Saying It Does Not Offer Any “Incremental TAM” And That Satellite Connectivity Remains An Inferior Medium
 Rohail Saleem • 
 Oct 29, 2026 at 06:34am EDT 
 Comments 
 Add to Preferred Sources
 T-Mobile remains unconvinced 
 How many times can SpaceX be jilted at the proverbial altar? T-Mobile's CEO has again rejected the idea of a Mobile Virtual Network Operator (MVNO) arrangement - where a wireless service provider does not own the underlying physical cellular network infrastructure - with SpaceX, terming it patently superfluous, especially as the cellular giant still sees "huge growth opportunities" in the urban areas of the US, where satellite coverage is limited.
 T-Mobile CEO on SpaceX's modus operandi: "Satellite is an inferior version of FWA with even more constraints in terms of things like what is the size of the beam"
 SpaceX's terrestrial spectrum mainly consists of around 15 MHz of unpaired nationwide Advanced Wireless Services-3 or AWS-3 spectrum band, around 40 MHz of nationwide AWS-4 spectrum, around 10 MHz of nationwide H-Block spectrum, and around 14 megahertz of paired spectrum in the 800 MHz band .
 Related Story SpaceX Tells FAA It Alone Expects 10,000 Launches A Year, As It Gears Up To Target $28.5 Trillion Market That Elon Musk Believes Is Inadequate 
 Even so, this terrestrial spectrum is not sufficient to allow SpaceX to start its own mobile service in urban areas, which means its most attractive option centers on entering into an MVNO with one of the so-called Big Three telecom players - AT&T, T-Mobile, or Verizon.
 However, sensing a direct threat from SpaceX's rapidly expanding cellular ambitions, all three carriers have refused to enter into an MVNO arrangement, forcing SpaceX to rely on its space-based 2 GHz of mid-band spectrum to serve as the backbone for a cellular network in the US, while its new 14 megahertz of spectrum in the 800 MHz band ensures that Starlink Mobile signals are able to penetrate buildings.
 Concurrently, SpaceX is trying to lease at least 80,000 different cell tower sites across the US, presumably setting aside $75,000 for each such site or $6 billion in total , and has received an approval from the FCC to launch as many as 15,000 V2 (Gen2) satellites that can connect directly to smartphones. It is also exploring small, low-power femtocell-type cellular base stations on existing Starlink dishes to avoid the massive upfront CapEx required for building cell towers and acquiring the appropriate spectrum.
 This brings us to the core of today's topic. T-Mobile's CEO, Srini Gopalan, delved into the contentious issue of an MVNO with SpaceX during Wednesday's earnings call , terming SpaceX's overarching strategy rather haphazard:
 "I saw your note as well in terms of the shape-shifting nature of SpaceX’s strategy. So it’s hard to refer to them now as a satellite provider or a satellite provider that is going to build terrestrial. So hard to think about whether this is SpaceX alone or all of satellites."
 Going to the heart of T-Mobile's reluctance, Gopalan declared that satellite-based connectivity is fundamentally inferior to the Fixed Wireless Access technology used by T-Mobile:
 "So let me answer that question in its broadest terms, right? Here’s the way we think about broadband. We’ve got a great product in FWA and really in many ways, except for some deep rural parts, satellite is an inferior version of FWA with even more constraints in terms of things like what is the size of the beam, right? So I don’t see the synergy there between FWA and satellite."
 "In many ways, two-thirds of our FWA customers come from dense urban areas. We see huge growth opportunities in those areas still, all under the fallow capacity model. So we don’t really see a synergistic opportunity with satellite providers, and that’s a broader piece."
 Basically, T-Mobile does not see any "incremental TAM" from entering into an MVNO arrangement with SpaceX:
 "I think it comes back to the philosophy with which we operate MVNOs, which is what is the incremental TAM that something opens out? And am I willing to get into a deal for the incremental TAM?"
 "If it’s a complementary product, I’m very happy to look at a resale arrangement, which is exactly what T-Satellite was, which gets built into it. But an MVNO is a wholly different thing. So I hope that clarifies where our head’s at on MVNOs and more broadly satellite."
 Gopalan also added that T-Satellite, which is currently powered by SpaceX, accounts for just 0.0002 percent of its total network usage .
 Finally, T-Mobile believes 6G is its next best opportunity , and sees "no space for an MVNO here because what additional capabilities does it give us? Why does it change our ability to compete?"
